concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: augmented reality
concepts.definition: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

defining_facts.text: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content.
Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains.
In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.
In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality (AR) can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.
The presence of many augmented reality (AR) applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.
Pokemon Go is a famous augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

Augmented reality (AR) is defined by the Merriam-Webster dictionary as an enhanced version of reality created by the use of technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.

The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.
An augmented reality (AR) system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: display
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a display or output device is used in a broad sense to mean any device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs, not only a visual display.
A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.
The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.

The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

concepts.name: sensor
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a sensor or input device is used in a broad sense to mean any tracking device that tracks the user's input and extracts information from the real world, with the discussion restricted to sensors that track the user's movements.
Tracking is also commonly called sensing; tracking is the more popular term, but the devices that enable tracking are more often called sensors than trackers.

The term sensor has two related but structurally different meanings: in a device or system, a sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals in a circuit; in the human body, human bodily sensors are body organs that convert a stimulus into neural impulses.

concepts.name: tracking
concepts.definition: In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

defining_facts.text: In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.
Tracking is an integral hardware component of an extended reality (XR) system.
Keeping track of motion in the physical world is a crucial part of any extended reality (XR) system, more importantly in virtual reality (VR) systems.
In virtual reality (VR), tracking is primarily about tracking the user's physical motion or input so that it can be translated into virtual motion in the virtual world.

In augmented reality (AR), tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in three-dimensional (3D) space with respect to an anchor in the real world, and it requires tracking the user's pose, position, and orientation as well as tracking moving real-world objects in the field of view.
Tracking is also commonly called sensing; tracking is the more popular term, but the devices that enable tracking are more often called sensors than trackers.
There are two broad ways to obtain input for tracking: inside-out and outside-in.
The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
In the tracking process, calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.
In the tracking process, registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked.

In the tracking process, integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.

In the tracking process, drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error.

Low-level libraries and frameworks are the augmented reality (AR) software category that requires the maximum skill from the developer because they provide access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an AR application.

ARToolKit provides marker-based tracking in its open-source version, while its commercial version, available from ARToolWorks, also supports tracking natural features on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques.
ARToolKit is primarily a tracking-support library: it provides functions that enable a developer to perform tracking and then carry out a related activity.

Many standard augmented reality (AR) toolkits or low-level libraries primarily provide tracking support but lack the features needed for realistic rendering of digital content over the real-world view and for interaction support.

To overcome the limitations of ARToolKit or other tracking-focused low-level libraries, a framework for augmented reality (AR) system development can be created by combining multiple libraries, especially libraries that provide interaction and realistic graphics support.

When ARToolKit is combined with a scene graph library, the scene graph library can take care of low-level object rendering, so the developer can focus on interaction between virtual objects while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking.

In an augmented reality (AR) example in which a phone detects a marker on a table and a three-dimensional (3D) cow object appears on the screen, the operation involves tracking, which recognizes the marker and its position, and three-dimensional (3D) registration, which creates and renders the cow at that position.

In the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, combining ARToolKit with Open Scene Graph (OSG) or Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) can perform the operations: ARToolKit handles tracking and three-dimensional (3D) registration, while OSG handles creation of the AR scene with the rendered cow.

In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect.

Examples of frameworks that combine tracking and rendering libraries include the Open Scene Graph (OSG) ART 3 library, which links ARToolKit for tracking support with OSG for real-time rendering features; Goblin XNA, which combines the ART tag tracking library with the Microsoft XNA game platform; and Metaio SDK plus OSG, in which the Metaio SDK provides augmented reality (AR) tracking technologies and OSG provides rendering support.

Mobile-specific augmented reality (AR) frameworks include ARToolKit for mobile, DroidAR, and Vuforia; DroidAR uses other sensors for tracking support, while Vuforia uses computer vision for tracking support.

concepts.name: registration
concepts.definition: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

defining_facts.text: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
In the tracking process, registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked.
Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation of the sensor or user and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented as theta at t = 0.

A simplifying assumption for understanding registration is that the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is turned on is taken as the initial orientation, with the initial alignment set to the forward direction.
Registration can be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags; it can also be performed without them using computer vision techniques, and the process is simpler when such aids are present.

Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.

concepts.name: pose
concepts.definition: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

defining_facts.text: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.
Vision-based trackers are more prevalent trackers that determine poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras.
The three main categories of optical sensors that can be deployed to detect or track a pose are infrared sensors, visible light sensors, and three-dimensional (3D) structure sensors.

In outside looking in infrared tracking, cameras placed in the environment rather than on the tracked object detect targets attached to the object and use them to determine the object's pose and position.
In inside looking out infrared tracking, the camera is mounted with the user and detects external targets, from which it estimates poses.

concepts.name: eye tracking
concepts.definition: Eye tracking devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically come integrated with headsets and track eye movements, including where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, helping the system understand the user's eye movement and infer what action to take.

defining_facts.text: Eye tracking devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically come integrated with headsets and track eye movements, including where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, helping the system understand the user's eye movement and infer what action to take.

The Midas touch problem in eye tracking-based input is the inability to differentiate an intentional gaze meant to select an object from a habitual blank gaze, so the system may select an object or perform an action even though the user did not intend to.

Multimodal input, which uses other forms of input in addition to eye tracking, is generally preferable over only eye tracking-based input for interacting with a system because eye tracking alone can cause objects to be selected or actions to be performed from unintentional gazes.
Eye-tracking systems can be part of other trackers and can be head-mounted or remotely attached to a display or an external display.

Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).
Eye-tracking systems typically track the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.

concepts.name: gyroscope
concepts.definition: An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs).

defining_facts.text: An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs).

In an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes.

Inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity, while the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation but can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

never_defined.definition: Electromagnetic trackers are non-contact position measurement devices in which a stationary transmitter in the environment produces a magnetic field, and a receiver attached to the headset moves with the head, and the receiver's real-time position is obtained from the magnetic field direction.

never_defined.name: antenna
never_defined.definition: In an electromagnetic tracker, the transmitter generally has three antennas that produce three orthogonal magnetic fields, and these fields generate alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC) in the receiver; the resulting currents help track the head's position relative to a fixed position in the environment.
